prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength to reach fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B030 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. Having read all eight round-1 statements and the chair's questions, I find the scientific case firmer, not weaker, because the reservations raised are the same ones from every side and none of them disputes that the achievement is real. The invention is the magic-wavelength lattice, which engineers the light shift away on the clock transition while suppressing Doppler and recoil effects and letting many neutral atoms be interrogated at once. The realization is the move to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, reproduced independently in several national laboratories. The one-sentence answer to the chair's first question is this: the 2005 prize rewarded the frequency comb as a ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 prize rewarded quantum control of single trapped systems, whereas the lattice clock is a different principle, a trap whose perturbation cancels by design for a large ensemble, and it was neither a corollary of those prizes nor covered by them. For me that sentence resolves the overlap worry, and I no longer count it as a reservation that could be disqualifying. On the citation, I support the scope that names the invention and the magic wavelength together with the 10^-18 level, because it states what was done and what was demonstrated without claiming the redefinition of the second. On the pending redefinition, I would not delay the award, and I am content for the committee to record that the case rests on demonstrated performance and independent agreement alone.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining reservation is attribution. Two names cannot represent Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, the JILA co-workers or the ion-clock groups, and I cannot settle from the supplied text how the committee should weigh them against Katori, whose conceptual proposal and early demonstrations are clear, and Ye, whose credit is the accuracy record, many-body clock physics and comparison technology. Pearce is right that this allocation is a judgement and not a clean fact, and I would say so openly rather than call it unassailable. A second reservation is that an instrument achievement has to be argued as physics. I accept Mehlig's point that ensemble averaging against quantum projection noise and the control of collisional and many-body shifts are physics in their own right, but the discovery content in fundamental tests (redshift, varying constants, dark matter) is still largely prospective in the sense that no violation has been found. Third, the redefinition of the second has not taken place, so the practical culmination is anticipated.

responses.point: Moved from B020 to B030, but lists the 2005 and 2012 overlap and the technology-versus-discovery character of the clock as his strongest reservations, saying B020 would be the cleaner discovery if the committee reads the prize record as saturated.
responses.response: I share your worry and tried to answer it directly in round 2. The overlap argument would carry weight if the lattice clock were an application of the comb or of ion control, but its defining step, cancelling the trap light shift at a magic wavelength for thousands of neutral atoms, is not contained in either. On discovery versus instrument, I would point to the many-body and light-shift physics that Mehlig and Lindroth describe, and to the fact that the clocks are already the most sensitive laboratory probes of gravitational redshift and of drifts in constants. I also agree with you that B020 is a genuine discovery, but you yourself leave its third name open and Pearce and I disagree on whether Spiering belongs, so I do not think B020 is ready to displace B030 on attribution. If you would move back to B020, I would like to hear which three names you would defend.

responses.point: Prefers B022 (Car and Parrinello) alone on the grounds of two-author clarity and forty years of independent use, but says he would not stand in the way of B030 or B058 and defers on lattice-clock priority.
responses.response: I accept the strength of your attribution argument and I do not want it lost: B022 has the cleanest credit on the list, and its impact is beyond question. My difficulty remains the Nobel criterion, which asks for a discovery or an invention in physics, and I think the committee has to decide the physics-versus-chemistry boundary before B022 can enter a configuration. I do not think the answer is obviously no, but only you and Mehlig ranked it in the opening round, and I would not want to see it lose in the vote only because that question was never resolved. I note your statement that you would not oppose B030, and I hope you will say in the vote whether you treat it as your single prize part or hold B022 as a competing configuration.

responses.point: Holds B030 first, argues that ensemble averaging against quantum projection noise and the control of many-body shifts make the clock physics and not only engineering, but says the overlap with the comb and trapped-ion prizes is close enough that it should not be treated as closed.
responses.response: Your statistical-physics argument is the best answer to the technology objection, and I would use it in the citation discussion. On the overlap, I think we differ less than it seems: the clock does use comb technology to count optical cycles, but so does nearly all modern optical metrology, and I do not believe dependence on a tool is the same as the tool's prize covering the result. Where I would not go as far as you is in treating the open attribution to other lattice-clock groups as only a footnote. I would ask the chair to record that Lemonde and Lisdat are not simply excluded and that the pair is a committee judgement.

responses.point: As chair, moved to B030 but asks that the Katori and Ye split be described as a judgement and not a clean fact, and keeps B020 as the case he would revert to if the attribution gap there looked smaller.
responses.response: I agree that the allocation should be called a judgement. Katori holds the proposal and the first demonstrations, and Ye holds the record accuracy, the many-body regime and the comparison technology, and a committee could reasonably have weighted these differently. My own view is that the two together are still the most defensible pair, since adding names would require cutting arbitrarily from Lemonde, Lisdat and Ludlow in the way the chair describes for B017. I would answer your B020 point the same way: I would accept B020 as a competing configuration only if you, Danielsson and Kroll can agree on a three-name credit including or excluding Spiering.

responses.point: Would not name Lemonde in the citation, accepts the redefinition of the second as a timing question and not a flaw in the science, and does not accept that the earlier metrology prizes cover the magic-wavelength lattice.
responses.response: I agree with you on the redefinition and on the overlap, and I would make the same exclusion in the citation wording: it names the two invented things, the magic-wavelength lattice and its realization at 1e-18, and says nothing about timekeeping policy. On Lemonde I am slightly less sure than you, because as someone outside atomic metrology I cannot tell how independent his group's early lattice-clock work was. You are better placed than I am to say whether the expert record supports excluding him, and that is the single piece of evidence beyond the supplied text that I would most want to see before the vote.

uncertainties: Whether the Katori and Ye pair holds up against the independent early lattice-clock contributions of Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and others, which I cannot settle from the supplied text and as an outsider to atomic metrology.
Whether other members who hold the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes will accept the one-sentence distinction I gave, or still treat it as a reservation.
Which of the citation scopes the committee will adopt, and whether naming the 10^-18 level makes the citation too tied to a number that other clocks may soon pass.

For my alternatives B004 and B058: the unresolved choice of three among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger for B004, and the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp attribution for B058. I have left B029 out of my alternatives because I should not weigh it.
statement.conflict_note: I am a professor at Chalmers and director of WACQT, with documented ties to Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum. Circuit QED (B029) is my own research area and Chalmers hosted researchers connected to the 2025 prize, so I should be recused from weighing B029, and I have removed it from my alternatives in this round. No specific personal or institutional connection to the B030 candidates (Katori, Ye), to B004 or to B058 is apparent from my profile, and I do not work in atomic metrology.
